chapter: New York bands and the first records
title: 'In a Mist' and Jack Kapp at Brunswick
summary: In the early 1930s he secretly recorded four-hammer marimba pieces for Brunswick; Jack Kapp tore up his contract and said it could never sell.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Yeah, I think that -- that the style -- all the things that I've done in music, I've been dictated by -- by the instrument.
Yeah.
I think it has to be.
Yeah.
And, even after that, when I --after that band broke up, I went to things that were comfortable for
the instrument.
Yeah.
Now, I mentioned it in a news story, I must say this, early -- in the early '30's, I'd made a few records for Jack Capp, up at Brunswick --
Yeah.
They were tinkly little things, --
YEAH.
-- I tried -- he wanted me to do --
I'm going to hold this off, just a second.
There we go. Red, you were going to tell me, you had something to tell me about -- In a Mist, hadn't you?

Oh, yes. I was telling you that in 19 -- I think it was in the early '30's, I recorded a few things for Brunswick, kind of a tinkly sort of xylophone solos, and they'd gone pretty well -- they were kind of little blues and little solo I'd written, couple of things I'd written for the day. But I really wanted to record some four-hammer things on marimba, which they wouldn't let me. So, I decided to go ahead and try it, see if I could get it in.

So, I had Herb Spencer doing a little cut out with a guitar, bass -- bass clarinet and I made it playing it on marimba. So I didn't think Jack would go for it, so we set the date late at night. At 11:00 o'clock at night, which they used to do in those days --
I remember, yes.
-- Brunswick, --
Yeah.

-- so, we went in the studio at 11:00 o'clock at night, and we just made it in a hurry, made it pretty well, got right on through it pretty good. So, I just packed up and went home and about two or three weeks later I get a call from Jack Capp and he says, 'Come up here, I want to see you.' So I go in, he said, 'What's the idea of recording stuff like this? He said I couldn't sell that within a million years, that stuff.' And meantime, he's tearing up my contract.

Slowly, very slowly. I knew it was my contract cause I recognized it. He said, 'I don't know how I'm going to get my money out of that,' he said, 'I'll probably send it -- maybe I can sell it to an English firm I know, they go for stuff like this, maybe it'll sell over there.'
